name: citor
baseline: oneTBB (also Taskflow, libfork, TooManyCooks, HPX in the same suite)
workload: Recursive fork-join suite (fibonacci, skynet 100M tasks, n-queens, matmul) on 64 threads in the independent tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite.
claimed_speedup: Mean ratio to best: citor 1.06x, libfork 1.18x, TooManyCooks 1.32x, TBB 3.25x, taskflow 3.34x (so about 3x lower mean ratio than TBB; derived from page data). Repo README says it tops the recursive fork-join summary.
tradeoffs: C++20, Linux x86_64 primary (Windows secondary), needs GCC 14+/Clang 19+; header-only; eight sync primitives (parallelFor, parallelReduce, forkJoin ...).
caveats: Suite is maintained by the author of a competing runtime (TooManyCooks), though citor is not his. OpenMP not in the suite. Ratios are a mean across tests, not per-test; the citor README itself says latency figures are hardware dependent.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ fork-join task scheduler faster than oneTBB fibonacci benchmark; opened tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks

name: ForkUnion
workload: N-body (512 bodies) dispatch latency and connected-components label propagation (84 fork-join rounds, ~27M edges) on every logical core.
claimed_speedup: N-body on 128x Intel SPR Linux, static: ForkUnion C++ 54 us vs OpenMP 115 us, Rayon 483 us, Taskflow 666 us. Connected components GTEPS (SPR): ForkUnion C++ 46.5 vs OpenMP 28.2, Rayon 8.5, Taskflow 25.1. README: about 3-6x faster than OpenMP, 12-16x faster than Rayon and Taskflow per parallel-for dispatch.
tradeoffs: Bulk-synchronous data-parallel loops only: no nested parallelism, futures, task graphs or exceptions; NUMA-aware; bindings for C, C++, Rust, Zig.
caveats: First-party benchmark; bench sources are in scripts/ but CPU models and compiler versions are incomplete, so not tier A. Not a work-stealing scheduler (it deliberately avoids stealing), so it is a niche win over parallel-for dispatch, not over TBB task scheduling. oneTBB not in the benchmark.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ fork-join task scheduler faster than oneTBB; result 'Beyond OpenMP in C++ & Rust' led to the repo

name: Staccato
baseline: Intel TBB 4.3 and Intel Cilk Plus 7.3
workload: fib(42), dfs 9^9 tree, matmul 3500x350, blkmul 4096x4096 on 56 threads.
claimed_speedup: README text only: improvement most noticeable on CPU-bound tasks (fib, dfs), memory-bound tasks almost unaffected. Exact numbers are only in PNG charts under docs/ which were not readable.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11, spawn/wait API, supports weak memory models.
caveats: Old baselines (TBB 4.3, Cilk Plus, now deprecated). No numeric claim in text; chart images only. Last commit date not confirmed, likely 2018 or earlier.

name: Nowa
baseline: Cilk Plus and TBB lock-based continuation stealing; OpenMP tasks (libomp)
workload: Fork/join benchmark suite on up to 256 hardware threads (IPDPS 2021 paper).
claimed_speedup: Wait-free runtime up to 1.64x faster than lock-based runtimes at 256 threads, 1.17x on average; 8.68x faster than OpenMP tasks (clang libomp) on average (snippet only, paper PDF not opened).
tradeoffs: Built on Fibril (cactus stack, continuation stealing, custom stack switching); research prototype; build via ./build.
caveats: Paper (IEEE IPDPS 2021) and Zenodo are EGRESS_BLOCKED; numbers come from WebSearch snippets, not opened. Mirror repo has no benchmark numbers in README. Original repo is on Zenodo record 4541475.

name: stealpool
baseline: central-queue thread pool and serial code (not TBB/OpenMP/Rayon)
workload: fib(36) cutoff 20, unbalanced tree, 1M empty tasks, reduce 16M doubles, parallel quicksort 20M ints.
claimed_speedup: 2.02x fib and 3.6x 1M empty tasks over central queue; parallel quicksort 589 ms vs 1507 ms std::sort.
tradeoffs: C++17 Chase-Lev deque work-stealing scheduler, small hobby project.
caveats: Does not compare to TBB, OpenMP or Rayon despite naming them. Noisy shared CI runner, no flags, no license shown. Included as a low-confidence data point.
